title: Pinpoint: Grounded Worldwide Image Geolocation via Cross-Source Retrieval and Reranking
claim: A query is embedded, used to retrieve a shortlist of candidates, then reranked by attention to produce a final prediction.
layout: 4 dashed panels, left-to-right, numbered stages, connectors labeled rerank and argmax
description: A four-stage left-to-right pipeline in numbered, dashed-border panels. Panel 1, Contrastive embedding, shows a query photo of a historic building passing through a trapezoid encoder labeled SigLIP2, with a source adapter and a shared trunk. It outputs a normalized query embedding z_q, drawn as a blue striped bar. A curved arrow carries this embedding to Panel 2, Shortlist retrieval. There, a reference database cylinder of image and GPS embeddings feeds a k-NN similarity search, drawn as a circle of blue dots around a red query point. This yields a merged top-K shortlist of thumbnails. Panel 3, Attention reranking, shows a token sequence of [CLS], query, image and support tokens. The tokens pass through a stacked Transformer encoder and produce rerank scores such as 2.81 and 1.04, with the argmax boxed in red. Panel 4, Final prediction, shows the selected anchor photo and a map pin with coordinates. Blue and red are the main colors.
caption: Overview of the Pinpoint inference pipeline. The query image is encoded by a frozen contrastive image tower and used to retrieve a top-k shortlist from the retrieval index, which is then rescored by an attention-based reranker that selects the final predicted geolocation.
abstract: Image geolocation aims to estimate where a photograph was taken from its visual content. At worldwide scale, this remains challenging because visual evidence is often ambiguous, diverse, and unevenly distributed. Prior work has typically treated geolocation of ordinary internet photos and street-view imagery as separate tasks, despite their complementary strengths: internet photos better match the appearance distribution of user-captured queries, while street-view imagery provides denser, geographically grounded coverage. We present Pinpoint, a retrieve-and-rerank architecture that combines both sources in a coarse-to-fine pipeline. A contrastive image-GPS embedder is trained on both user-uploaded Flickr photos and street-view imagery, learning a shared image-GPS embedding space that is used to retrieve candidate locations. An attention-based reranker then rescores retrieved candidates by combining candidate-level visual and GPS features with cross-source evidence from nearby locations to ground the prediction. Unlike recent prior work, Pinpoint does not rely on multimodal large-language models, making inference faster and more reproducible. Pinpoint achieves state-of-the-art results across all metrics on standard benchmarks for internet photos (IM2GPS3k and YFCC4k) and street-view imagery (OSV-5M).
